title: Recent Advances in Integrated Photonic Molecules
content: Photonic molecules are systems of coupled optical resonators, or of deliberately coupled modes within one resonator, whose collective states have engineered frequencies, lifetimes and optical access. Integration on silicon, silicon nitride, thin-film lithium niobate and hybrid platforms has turned them from spectroscopic objects into circuit elements for filtering, frequency conversion, nonlinear light generation, lasing and sensing. This review covers the physics and the state of the art of integrated photonic molecules. We first  introduce the temporal coupled-mode description of a two-resonator molecule and the quantities used to characterize it: mode splitting, linewidth and their ratio. We then review each platform: thermally tuned and photonic-crystal molecules in silicon for compact spectral processing, spectrometry and sensing; low-loss silicon nitride molecules for soliton and  parametric generation, squeezed light and narrow-linewidth Brillouin lasing; and electro-optic molecules in lithium niobate and hybrid stacks for programmable two-level dynamics, frequency shifting, comb generation and transduction. Non-Hermitian and active molecules, including exceptional-point devices and coupled lasers, are treated  separately. Comparison tables collect the reported metrics together with their operating conditions. We close with the open problems of calibration, stability and packaging and with  prospects in microwave photonics and quantum technologies.
